pr.title: Add project ios to build a branch's iOS app and put it on a device
pr.head: fc7df3d3afd6793d9e1257c99ba46412ff23534d

summary: Projector's inbox lets an agent ask the person to test a change on their phone, with a start button whose press runs one action, such as installing a build. Until now Projector gave the agent nothing to build or install with, so each iOS repository wrote its own script. This pull request adds project ios, a command group that builds any branch or pull request of a repository's iOS app without touching the person's checkout, puts it on their iPhone, iPad, or Mac, and brings the device's crash reports and log back.

It is the first layer of a stack. The plan, docs/projects/ios/readme.md, sits in the pull request below, and the skill paragraphs that tell an agent how to use the command sit in the one above. The plan moves from ready to in-progress here, and stays there until the person runs a real build on a real iPhone.

CommandWhat it does
build <branch-or-number>Fetches the head into Projector's own worktree, builds it, keeps a copy of the app for that target, then installs and opens it. --no-install stops after the build.
install [<target>]Installs and opens that target's kept build, or the newest one.
devices [--json]Lists paired devices and whether each can take an install.
crashesCopies the app's three newest crash reports to the Desktop and summarizes each.
logs [--last 5m]Writes the app's recent log lines to a new file on the Desktop.
cleanupRemoves the worktree, DerivedData, and every kept build.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Target: the branch name or pull request number the person passes to build. Each target keeps its own build.
  • Kept build: a copy of the built .app under builds/<App>/<key>/, with a build.json record of the app, commit, and bundle ID.
  • Key: the folder name for a target, pr-12 for a pull request and branch- plus the percent-encoded branch name, such as branch-feature%2Flogin.
  • Trusted head: a pull request head that review.trusted_head accepts. It lives in this repository, and its author and every commit's author is the operator or has write access.
  • DerivedData: Xcode's build folder. One shared folder per repository lets a branch switch rebuild only what changed.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html: The plan's reviews settled the trust rule, the log filter, how builds are copied, the target keys, the Codex allow list, and the device flags. The first review of this layer found no blocking problem and listed five suggestions, such as passing the bundle ID to osascript as an argument rather than inside the script.

groups.title: The project ios module
groups.kicker: Device choice, the lock, the worktree, the build, kept builds, install, crashes, logs, and cleanup
intro: ios.py is a port of a shell script one repository used for device tests, rewritten on the standard library. Each command follows the same order: check that xcrun and xcodebuild exist, pick the device, take the repository's lock, then do the work. Picking the device before the build means a phone that cannot take the install fails in seconds rather than after a ten-minute build.

All branches share one worktree and one DerivedData folder, so builds run one at a time under an fcntl.flock lock. After each build, the app is copied into a folder for its target, so install 12 installs pull request 12's build even after another agent built something else. That is what lets the inbox's start button install the change its request describes.

xcodebuild runs the project's build scripts as the person. So before it fetches a pull request, build asks review.trusted_head, the same rule a Projector review uses, and refuses an untrusted head with exit 65 unless the person passes --allow-untrusted. A branch name is trusted, because only an account with write access can push a branch to the repository.

checks.text: The tests stand in for xcrun, xcodebuild, osascript, open, log, sudo, and cp with one script on PATH, and run Git for real against a bare origin, so they run on Linux with no Xcode. No test touches a real device.

files.note: The whole command. Each section header in the file, such as # Kept builds, matches one step of the plan's build flow.

checks.text: The trust check runs before any fetch. The fetch at line 235 also refuses a head that moved after the check, so a commit pushed in between is never built.

When the worktree already exists, the fetch and the checkout run through the worktree itself, which puts the commit into whichever clone created it. A worktree whose clone was deleted makes rev-parse fail, and is removed and made again from this clone.

On a Mac, cp -cR makes an APFS clone that costs no time or space. Elsewhere, such as on CI's Linux runner, the copy is a plain copytree. The choice follows sys.platform, so Linux never depends on what its cp does with -c.

The bundle ID is placed inside the AppleScript source here and at line 525. It comes from the build settings of a head that was trusted or that the person allowed. The review suggested passing it as an argument instead, so a strange bundle ID cannot change the script.

The log filter keeps the bundle ID, its dotted children, and the bundle ID without its last part only when that leaves three or more parts. So com.example.myapp.dev also matches com.example.myapp, and no bundle ID ever matches the vendor prefix com.example.

Any exit from the collect, a Ctrl-C included, deletes the claimed log file, and the finally deletes the archive, which holds the whole device's log. The tests exercise the failed collect, not the Ctrl-C.
cleanup keeps the lock file. Deleting it while another run waits on it would let a third run lock a new file and build at the same time.

files.note: One test for each row of the plan's acceptance table, named after the behavior it checks.

groups.title: Helpers shared with reviews
groups.kicker: Two small refactors so the command reuses what reviews already do
intro: Reviews already fetch a pull request's head and keep state under Projector's state folder. Two functions move out so ios.py can call them. Neither changes what a review does.

files.note: head_ref picks the branch for a head in this repository and refs/pull/<n>/head for a fork. state_home names $XDG_STATE_HOME/projector, or ~/.local/state/projector without it.

groups.title: The command line and its settings
groups.kicker: The argparse tree for project ios, and three new settings
intro: add_ios_parser builds the subcommands, and run_ios reads the settings and calls into ios.py. The settings let a repository that does not follow the naming convention name its app, its Xcode project, and where crash reports and logs go.

files.note: Every subcommand parser sets allow_abbrev=False, so --allow-unt is an error rather than a spelling the ask rule would miss.

checks.text: This comment is why the ask rule works. Without allow_abbrev=False, argparse accepts any unique prefix of --allow-untrusted, and the rule matches only the full word.

groups.title: Permission rules for agents
groups.kicker: One new ask rule in Claude Code, and four allowed commands in Codex
intro: project init writes the rules that decide which project commands an agent may run without asking. In Claude Code every project command is allowed, so the new rule Bash(project ios *allow-untrusted*) makes Claude Code ask before building an untrusted head.

Codex allows commands by name and runs an allowed command outside its sandbox. So Codex allows only the four project ios commands that run no repository code: devices, install, crashes, and cleanup. It still asks for build, which runs the repository's build scripts, and for logs, which runs sudo.

files.note: The rule in ASK, the new CODEX_ALLOW entry, and the explanations that name them.
New rows in DECISIONS give each command's decision in both hosts, and a new test refuses each abbreviation of --allow-untrusted.
